title: Eating Five Fruits and Vegetables a Day May Not Be Enough to Protect Your Heart, Major Study Finds
excerpt: A new analysis of over 30,000 adults reveals that fewer than one in four people eating the recommended five daily servings of fruits and vegetables actually get enough flavanols to reduce cardiovascular risk — and the fix may already be in your chai cup
body:
For decades, the "five-a-day" rule has been the gold standard of dietary advice: eat five servings of fruits and vegetables and your body will thank you. But a sweeping new study published this week in the journal *Food & Function* suggests that for heart health specifically, five-a-day is necessary but far from sufficient. The real question, researchers say, is not how many servings you eat — but what is *in* them.

An international team led by Dr Javier Ottaviani of the University of Reading, with collaborators at Harvard Medical School, UC Davis, and Mars Inc., analysed dietary data from more than 30,000 adults across the United States and the United Kingdom. Their finding is striking: fewer than 25 per cent of people who meet the five-a-day guideline actually consume the 500 milligrams of flavanols per day associated with meaningful cardiovascular protection.

## What Are Flavanols and Why Do They Matter?

Flavanols are a subclass of plant-derived compounds called flavonoids, found in varying concentrations across fruits, vegetables, tea, and cocoa. Unlike vitamins that have well-established recommended daily intakes, flavanols have flown under the dietary radar — until now.

The new study draws heavily on results from the landmark COSMOS trial (Cocoa Supplement and Multivitamin Outcomes Study), a randomised controlled trial of more than 21,000 older adults. COSMOS found that a daily intake of 500mg of flavanols was associated with a 27 per cent reduction in cardiovascular disease mortality. That is a figure comparable to some pharmaceutical interventions, yet it comes from food.

"People assume that meeting the five-a-day target automatically delivers all the bioactive compounds they need," said Professor Gunter Kuhnle, a co-author and nutritional scientist at the University of Reading. "Our data show that's simply not the case for flavanols. The type and preparation of fruits and vegetables matters enormously."

## The Gap Between Guidelines and Reality

The researchers matched dietary records with food composition databases to estimate actual flavanol intake. They found that the average adult consuming five servings of fruit and vegetables gets roughly 300-350mg of flavanols per day — well short of the 500mg threshold.

The shortfall exists because not all produce is created equal in flavanol content. Lettuce, cucumbers, carrots, and bananas — some of the most commonly consumed items — are relatively low in flavanols. Meanwhile, berries, apples eaten with skin, green tea, and cocoa products are concentrated sources but feature less frequently in Western diets.

The top dietary sources of flavanols, ranked by concentration per typical serving, include:

- **Green tea**: approximately 200mg per cup
- **Blackberries**: approximately 130mg per cup
- **Apples with skin**: approximately 60mg per medium apple
- **Broad beans (fava beans)**: approximately 55mg per half-cup
- **Plums**: approximately 45mg per two fruits
- **Dark chocolate (70%+ cocoa)**: approximately 40mg per 30g square

## A Hidden Advantage in South Asian Kitchens

For the Indian diaspora, the findings carry a quietly encouraging message. Several foods that rank highest for flavanol content are already embedded in South Asian dietary traditions.

Green tea and its close relatives — including matcha and the light teas served across North and East India — deliver among the highest flavanol concentrations of any food. A household that drinks two to three cups of green tea daily could be meeting two-thirds of the 500mg target from tea alone.

Broad beans, widely consumed in Bengal and South India as *sheem* or *avarakkai*, are another potent source. Apples, a popular fruit across Indian households in the US, contribute meaningfully when eaten with skin rather than peeled — a distinction that South Asian families often overlook.

Dark berries, increasingly available at Indian grocery stores in the US and UK, and seasonal fruits like plums and *jamun* (black plum) round out a diet that could comfortably hit the flavanol target without any supplements.

"If you're already drinking green tea and eating seasonal fruit with the skin on, you may be closer to optimal flavanol intake than someone eating five salads a day," said Dr Ottaviani.

## Supplements Are Not the Only Answer

The study comes at a time when the supplement industry is aggressively marketing flavanol and cocoa extract capsules, often at premium prices. The researchers caution that while supplements can help, whole-food sources offer additional fibre, vitamins, and synergistic compounds that capsules cannot replicate.

The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics in the US has not yet established an official recommended daily intake for flavanols, though a 2022 expert panel convened by Mars and academic collaborators proposed 400-600mg as a provisional target. The new study strengthens the case for formal guidelines.

## What This Means for Your Plate

The practical takeaway is not to abandon the five-a-day principle but to be more strategic about which five you choose. Swapping a side salad for a cup of green tea and a handful of blackberries, for instance, could more than double your flavanol intake without adding calories.

For NRI families trying to balance Indian and Western dietary patterns, the study validates a simple shift: lean into the tea-and-fruit traditions that already exist in South Asian culture, and treat them not as indulgences but as cardiovascular medicine hiding in plain sight.

*Sources: Food & Function (DOI: 10.1039/D6FO00867D), University of Reading press release, COSMOS trial data, Fox News Health, The Times*
